title: One Writing Skill, Lots of Examples, and the Occasional Jolly Rancher
author: Jennifer Haber
summary: Jennifer Haber walks through a seventh-grade lesson on one narrow writing skill: giving context before a quotation in a literary analysis essay. She argues that sophisticated writing must be taught explicitly, one skill at a time, rather than assumed to arrive with age. Using a line from her retelling of the Epic of Gilgamesh, she contrasts weak and strong context, introduces five ways to provide context, and has students rate four versions of the same quotation on a 1 to 4 scale. The shared numbers then give her a quick vocabulary for revision conferences. She pairs the lesson with built-in repetition, notably a Friday review game, so that skills are retrieved long after first being taught.
points: Haber teaches essay writing as separate, modelled and practised skills, with the essay assembled in class instead of at home.
Contrasting weak context ('In the story, it says') with strong context makes the target visible; the strong version names the speaker, the situation and the stakes in one sentence.
A 1 to 4 rating scale, applied to four versions of the same quotation, trains students to judge context and gives teacher and student a shared revision language.
Five named approaches (before, during, purpose, comparison, contrast) come with sentence starters on a chart students keep for later grades.
Repetition is built into routines such as end-of-test questions and a Friday 'Wheel of Knowledge' where students may always pass, and shy students end up volunteering.
quotes: I don’t expect students to know how to write with greater sophistication simply because they’ve gotten older. I have to teach them how.
When I teach essay writing, I break the process into individual lessons rather than expecting students to tackle everything at once.
Students need to give the reader enough information about the situation surrounding the moment they're quoting so that the quotation makes sense.
The second version identifies the speaker, explains what's happening, and prepares the reader to understand the quotation. It does all of that in one sentence.
This is where students begin to see that providing context isn’t just about putting a sentence before a quotation. It’s about making that sentence do something useful.
I can sit beside a student, point to the context leading into their quotation, and ask, “What number do you think this is?
Teaching a skill once doesn’t mean students will remember it.
By the end of the year, it’s rare for even my shyest students to pass.
